## Game Dev Recap: Making Viral Games

So, I recorded a gamedev podcast with Gavin Eisenbeiss, also known as TwoStar, the creator of Choo Choo Charles and currently working on CuffBust, and we talked about how to make viral video games.
The way Gavin does this is by designing his games for content creators.
They want to get a lot of views, so they play the games that give them the most views.
They essentially play a bunch of different games on their channel and check out which of their videos does the best, so then they play more of that game.
Content creators also all watch each other, so this way you can go super duper viral if your game is popular with content creators.
And designing for content creators means you need their videos to do well, and that by proxy means you are designing for the viewers, essentially.
What keeps viewers watching?
So, this is a bit of a different approach to game development. You're not so much thinking about the players, you're thinking about the viewers.
You need instant conflict, you need your game to be easy to understand, you can't have any flow breakers or interruptions, you need a good tension curve with tension and relief, and you need longer tension and story arcs so you don't have any click-off points.
And a good example for this is, for example, boss fights, and another example Gavin gave was chase scenes.
Now you might be like, what the hell, why am I designing my game just to be fun to watch? I want it to be fun to play.
And luckily there are a lot of overlaps, but there are also a couple of disconnects.
Usually, you know, if your game has constant flow, good tension, that's not just fun to watch, that's also fun to play.
But there are also some games where, for example, that are very low on conflict or that have constant action, that can be fun to play, but aren't very fun to watch, especially this constant action thing I thought was an interesting point.
Because if there's too much action all of the time, it almost becomes a little bit numbing.
You would expect this to do well with viewers, but it actually doesn't.
This is an image Gavin shared with me, this is how he designs his games.
He tries to build them on human instinct, so survival, fight or flight type responses.
And then the next thing he looks at is nostalgia, so long known concepts, and familiarity and readability, so known concepts.
And then he builds character styles or brand and game recognition on top of that.
So you're essentially building new stuff, your own personalized stuff on top of known stuff.
And I think this way you get a good balance of, it feels familiar, but there's still something new to it.
And then the cherry on top is basically mass contentability, replayable, farmable.
So if your game is already going viral, this can make it go even more viral, because if content creators want to play it and there is more to play, then they will play more of it.
Gavin did a really good job with this new game CuffBust, so he essentially has a line of content creators lined up who want to play his game.

## 40 Truths You Must Know Before You Play my Game „Will You Snail?“
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Yik6vD3EaUc

Here are 40 things you should know about my game Will You Snail before you play it. I want to make sure you know exactly what you're getting yourself into. Minor spoiler warning of course because I'm showing you all the basics of the game. Number one, Will You Snail is a unique platformer where an evil AI predicts your movement. Wherever the AI thinks you will go, it'll spawn a trap to intercept you. In the game you dodge AI spawned traps, solve simple puzzles, uncover the secrets of the simulation. Oh, and endure the AI making fun of you when you mess up of course. You control a cute little snail called Shelly and the evil AI is called Squid. I recorded over 1000 voice lines for Squid which makes sure you can comment on a lot of different scenarios. Therefore, even though Will You Snail is a pure single player game, it doesn't really feel like you're playing it alone. The AI predictions are used to control all kinds of traps and enemies in the game. From spikes, jellyfish, to projectiles, to laser beams. All are spawned and moved depending on where the AI thinks you will go. Every now and then there are some enemies that don't do that but that's more the exception than the rule. The game is relatively short, your first playthrough will likely take somewhere between 4 and 6 hours. If you wanna keep playing after that, that's certainly possible though. With achievements, collectibles, secrets, replaying levels on higher difficulties and so on. Some of my playtesters have already sunk hundreds of hours into this game. It has an okay amount of replay value I'd say. The game releases Wednesday, March 9th, 2022, which at the point of uploading this is in a few days. If you're watching this video after March 9th, then lucky you, because that means the game is already out on Steam, Nintendo Switch, PlayStation, and Xbox. At the launch we're currently aiming for a price tag of 14.99 USD or 12.49 EUR. Just keep in mind that this is not a guarantee that the price will stay like that forever of course. You only need 3 buttons to play the game, left, right, and jump. There are no special movement abilities besides that, it's pure platforming. Even though the game's short, there's a ton of variety in the game. From shooter levels, to racing levels, to tower defense levels, to basketball levels. It's basically a lot of interesting ideas packed into a short but hopefully fun single player experience. The story in Will You Snail is mostly told using these dialogue files here, so there is a little bit of reading involved. But no worries, it's not too much. Will You Snail is meant to be fairly difficult, but due to the difficulty settings and assist features, pretty much everybody will still finish it in less than 6 hours or so. That being said, you'll certainly enjoy this game a lot more if you like difficult platforming stuff. Will You Snail is not a game for everybody. I really like this honest marketing approach, which is why on the Steam page I have this little test you can do to figure out if I think you'd like the game or not. At launch, the game texts and subtitles will probably be available on all of these languages here. We're still constantly working on adding more text languages though, and if you'd like to help with that, you're more than welcome to join the translator team on the Will You Snail Discord group. Another thing that seems to disappoint some of the people I've talked to is that there is no machine learning involved in the AI. It's just a very typical hard-coded game AI following simple predefined rules. The way the AI works is very simple. I just simulate a second of the snail's movement, see where it ends up, and then reset it back to its original position. The reason Squid sometimes calls you snail and sometimes human is because he knows the snail is controlled by a human. ## Can We Make This Button Fun To Press?
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7L1B5YaxxoA

This is a button and I'm wondering can we make it fun to press the button? Cause let's be honest, pressing buttons is kind of a lame activity. As an experiment, unplug your controller and see for how long it stays interesting to press those stupid little buttons. Spoiler, not very long. The first reason why that is the case is impact. We humans like having an impact on our environment because it gives us a feeling of control and power. Destroying things is only so much fun because it gives you a lot of impact quickly and without a lot of effort, which makes you feel important and powerful. Not having any impact on your environment usually feels like a waste of time. So let's start by giving our button some impact. Whenever you press it, the circle next to it lights up. We have some impact now. Wow! But why is it still not fun? Probably not enough impact yet. So I decided to make the circle rotate around the button and whenever you press the button, it stops. You already get a feeling of control now because you get to decide when the circle moves and when it doesn't. And that impact is already big enough to create a little bit of fun. There's still a big difference though. Destroying an object in real life has a lot more lasting consequences. There's no bringing that, whatever that was, back to normal, which makes its destruction feel more meaningful than a temporary circle motion on a screen. Writing something with a pencil on a piece of paper doesn't feel nearly as meaningful as writing with a permanent marker on a shelf, right? Lasting consequences are more fun. So let's give our button some lasting consequences. Holding the button creates a bubble and releasing it shoots it away. And I have to say, it worked. It's a lot more fun now. It almost feels like drawing an image. I even decided to give the button some knockback when firing, which made it even better. Anything that adds additional impact to your actions is usually a good thing. By the way, do you know what people really like to have an impact on? Other people. When you make a move in chess, your impact is not just that the piece is standing in a different position now. The far bigger impact you have is being able to trigger thoughts, emotions, and reactions from your opponent. Another kind of impact is reward. If somebody told me that I'd get a piece of chocolate every time I press a button, I'd probably press that button quite a lot because I like chocolate and it releases dopamine in my dummy little brain. While we cannot do that, there are a lot of other things we can use as chocolate in video games. The two most obvious ones are acoustic rewards and eye candy. Hell, there are entire YouTube channels centered around the creation of satisfying sounds because sounds can really be quite addicting. In my case, I just used a free program called BFXR to create some sound effects really quick. They're not even all that good, but the difference it makes is still absolutely remarkable. Let's also add some eye candy in the form of particles, some wobble and various shaking effects. Haptic rewards like controller rumble work as well. So far, we're still just adding additional impact to our button. That is because reward and impact are very closely related. A good reward has to have some sort of impact and impact almost always feels quite rewarding. The same rules apply. Lasting rewards tend to feel more valuable. A classic example for that in games would be an XP bar. Every time you fire a projectile, you get XP. When the bar is full, you level up and the higher your level, the more projectiles you shoot at once. The additional projectiles then lead to you having even more impact and eye candy to look at. So this is definitely both a desirable as well as a lasting reward. What's interesting about rewards is that artificially delaying them a bit can often make them even more desirable. One of the reasons why loot boxes often have quite prolonged opening animations. And there's yet another way to make rewards feel even more rewarding. Randomness. So let's try that. Let's randomize the XP values and tada! We have turned our button into an abusive gambling game. Yay! Morally questionable, but I'm not gonna lie. It is more exciting and keeps you pressing those buttons for a while. So that's our first segment. Impact and reward are more than enough to make something fun. Look at this. All of these activities require entirely different body motions, but they're fun for the same reason. Challenge. Yeah, even something as simple as a button press can provide you with enough challenge to keep you entertained for thousands of hours. I can't be the only one who's amazed by that, am I? The problem with challenge is that too much of it feels stressful and frustrating. Too little of it feels boring. If you want people to have fun with your challenge, you have to keep them between the two, which is hard to pull off. Mainly because people are just so different from one another. I added some enemies that can only be defeated by projectiles that are big enough. Projectiles that are too small compared to the enemies are absorbed completely without dealing any damage. This makes for a surprisingly compelling challenge that is all about timing, positioning, and even a little bit of planning. I also attached the XP reward to destroying enemies because attaching rewards to challenges is a sensible thing to do, I guess. A good challenge should also feel fair and provide you with plenty of feedback on how well you're doing. Our game already somewhat fulfills those two requirements, so let's just leave it at that. The game feels pretty fun by now, and I can't stop pressing the button! Help me! That is the power of challenge. Very, very powerful tool for creating fun. There's just one more missing piece in the puzzle. Fantasy. We humans have the amazing ability to empathize with almost everybody and everything. We love to wonder what it must be like to explore space in our spaceship, to go on a journey, meet new friends. You're in a spaceship now. The owners of the spaceship like having fun, okay? That's why they wrote fun on the spaceship. And just like that, you're not pressing a random button anymore. We associate these sounds with experiences, feelings and emotions, and this is also how nostalgia works. And that's not because these sounds are in any way special or more memorable than others, but we remember these sounds just because they accompanied our experiences and journeys all the time. When our headphones or speakers break and we can't hear these sounds and noises that were there with us all the time, it feels lonely, obviously. But it also feels lonely because we need these sounds for immersion, and this is actually a far more important point here. Immersion is what we call when we get drawn into these virtual worlds. Immersion is what we call when we completely forget that we're actually not in a forest full of cannibals. It's when our perceived reality gets completely overtaken by worlds that actually aren't real. To keep it brief, to achieve a rich and immersive experience, we game developers have multiple so-called sensory channels to make something feel more real and believable. We currently mostly use two or three of them, that being our eyes for visual information, our ears for auditory information, and in some cases even our hands in the case of vibrating controllers, for example. All of these non-stop inputs of information constantly help us to interact with these digital worlds, and when you can interact with something, it's basically real. According to many, many people in the game development community and outside of it, sounds are actually much more helpful for good, immersive experiences than equally well-crafted visuals. And I myself, as a sound designer, obviously agree. But on top of helping to build a believable atmosphere, sounds also help to give feedback to the player. With the help of sounds and noises, we simply get another layer of feedback, which helps us to understand the world around us and they make sure we always know what's going on. Vision keeping in game development is super important because with a more coherent vision you can also make a more coherent game. It will be a lot easier to stand out from the rest and you will also hopefully sell a lot more copies. That's why in my opinion every game developer should try to become really good at vision keeping and this is where I have to admit that I completely failed at that in my current indie game project Will You Snail. If you want to see how I failed, why I failed, what went wrong then check out the video I made a couple of weeks ago. This is basically a follow-up video to that. My top eight takeaways for how you can maneuver yourself out of a situation like this. Let's dive into it. Tip number one is try to get clarity about what your game is as early as possible or in other words try to find a vision for your game as early as possible. Pretty much did that for Will You Snail. Will You Snail was supposed to be a funky rage game where you fight an AI. Everything done correctly here? Nice. Tip number two is something I've learned from making Islanders and that is that having visual prototypes as well as gameplay prototypes really helps to define a vision for your game and also to keep a vision for your game. At some point in the development of Islanders, Friedemann made a really cool visual prototype that basically helped the entire team to understand what we are about to make. It helped to eliminate all misunderstandings because it was basically showing how the finished game is going to look like. You even could even place a couple of buildings. The game wasn't really working yet but it was just a little visual mock-up and that was absolutely fantastic for vision keeping. For Will You Snail I did not do that. I skipped out on pre-production entirely which is something you should not do. ## My Game Has An Identity Crisis! (Devlog)
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e0fy6MyCkoU

What do you do if your indie game has an identity crisis? And with that I mean your game doesn't really know what it is or where it belongs. If you are making indie games this will probably happen to you as well sooner or later. If you don't realize it's happening or if you don't do anything about it, it can be absolutely detrimental for your game. And the worst part is I don't even know myself how to deal with it. I have a couple of ideas and thoughts that I want to share with you, but honestly, I don't know what to do right now, so maybe you can help me out as well. Who knows. Now guess why I'm bringing this whole topic up. I've been working on a game called Will You Snail for quite a while now. And you guessed it, it has an identity crisis. If we don't manage to fix it, I'm pretty sure it will fall flat on its face. So from my perspective it's obviously pretty urgent. I'm determined to fix it. The question is just, is it even possible? And if yes, how? Would it even make sense? Or should I just abandon the project and start over with something else? All very tricky questions that I hope to find an answer for in this video, but let's start from the beginning. How do you know your game has an identity crisis? For me it all comes down to one simple question. What is your game? If you can't answer that question, your game has an identity crisis. About one year ago, Will You Snail started out as a funny little rage game where an AI tries to predict your movement and places spikes in real time in order to destroy you. And you have to make it to the other side of the level, which is extremely frustrating. As I wanted to make it a little more fun, the game turned more and more into a skill-based platformer, which was more fun to play but also felt a lot more generic and boring. And that's why I started sprinkling in some creative 2D indie game craziness. I added funky tower defense levels, combat levels, puzzle levels. There are levels where you have to dance and hit button prompts while dodging other stuff. And there's even a level where you have to fight the snowman mafia. I just added so many creative things that I felt like it didn't really make sense to make this game exclusively for super skilled platformer fanatics. I wanted the game to be accessible for a wider audience now, so I added difficulty settings, which changed the identity of the game again to a very funky and creative 2D platformer that can hopefully be enjoyed by everybody. On top of all of that, I didn't want to lose track of the initial idea for the game, which was very centered around the AI. So I did a bit of worldbuilding and I think I started telling a pretty interesting story about AI, about the future of AI. However, what I didn't realize during all of this is that I was dragging the game into too many directions. And now I'm left with a little bit of a mess. Is my game a rage game? A skill-based platformer? A creative platformer for everybody? Or a story-based game about AI? Now, I'm pretty sure the first question that comes up is, why not all of these things? And I feel like the main problem here is that all of these approaches have fundamentally different target audiences. Will You Snail as a rage game, for example, would be meant for content creators and their viewers, for people who like extreme challenges and for people who like to scream a lot. Whereas Will You Snail as a skill-based platformer would have to be quite a bit more forgiving and less unfair. The creative indie game platformer for everybody approach doesn't really go together with the rage game approach or the skill-based platformer approach either. And if you're just interested in an interesting story about AI, then a lot of difficult platforming definitely sounds like a hindrance as well. My current solution for those conflicts at the moment are difficulty settings. I just have one rage mode, one very hard mode for platforming, and then another easier mode for those who just want to enjoy the creative levels and the story. Does that mean the problem is solved now? Unfortunately not, because if you try to do so many things at once, yes, you can do all of them decently, but none of them will be truly excellent, and in the end, none of your target audiences will be truly satisfied. In my opinion, it is way better to focus on one thing, on one target audience, instead of spreading yourself too thin. That means you can deliver a way higher quality experience, and on top of that, which might be even more important, it makes marketing a lot easier. If you yourself are confused about what your game is and who it is for, then your potential customers will be confused about that as well, and move on to another game that better fits their current needs. Hmm, okay, but does that really mean I have to say goodbye to three of those approaches and only pick one? No, that is not the case either, because obviously we can keep the other ones in as nuances, but I definitely think we need one approach to focus on, one approach to really polish out, and one that we can use as a marketing angle later on. So now that we know which options there are, let's go through them one by one, let's talk about their advantages, their disadvantages, and what I would have to do in order to make them happen. First of all, Rage Mode. The advantages of turning Will You Snail into a Rage Game would be that it would be relatively easy to do, low effort, and we would be finished very soon, wouldn't require a lot of changes in terms of gameplay, and it would be a relatively unique Rage Game as well, plus it will be relatively attractive for content creators. On the minus side, however, this would lock out a huge majority of the player base, and could basically only be enjoyed by a handful of people that really enjoy Rage Games. What I would do if I went for this approach is I would try to create a good viewing experience, I would remove the difficulty settings, because once again I think difficulty settings don't go together with Rage Games at all. Hey, this is Jonas, I'm one of the developers of Islanders, and here's everything you need to know about our game condensed into a hopefully very short and interesting video. Islanders is a minimalist strategy game about building cities on beautiful islands. What we wanted to create is a builder game that can be enjoyed and played by almost anybody. The game will cost 5 bucks on launch, and it will come out April 4th, depending on when you watch this video. Might already be out. Islanders is a high score game where you gain points by placing buildings, and when you place a building you see a big number on top of it showing you how many points you'll get for placing it here. The amount of points you get for placing a building depends on its surroundings. A lumberjack, for example, earns one point for every tree in range, but loses six points for every other lumberjack in range. And when placing a building, the small numbers show you exactly where your points are coming from. The only resource in Islanders are the buildings in your inventory. You lose the game when you run out of buildings, or put differently, when your inventory is empty. Your building inventory gets a refill every time you reach a certain score, it's very simple, and the amount of points you need to collect in order to get a new set of buildings is displayed in the bottom left corner. Every time you get a set of new buildings, you can choose between two options, and whenever you decide for one option, the pack will still contain a couple of the buildings you chose earlier. So it's basically like deck building, but with buildings. ## 3 Most Powerful Fun Hacks In Game Design
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MLCAqlPGV_k

Here are three fun hacks for game design that basically instantly make your indie games a lot more fun to play. I know that sounds too good to be true, so in order to prove my point, I will transform this boring clicker game into a super addicting game. If you wanna see that happen, stick around. All three of these techniques are pretty much double-edged swords. Yes, they can make your game a lot better, but they can also make your game a lot worse if you're not careful. So that's why I think it's important to talk about them. Here we go. The first fun hack is multiplayer. Pretty much every game is more fun when you play it with a friend. In the first draft of my clicker game, you just had to click a button 100 times in order to win. It's very basic, and I hope we can all agree that this is not a very good or a very intelligent game system. So even if we take a crappy game system like this, what happens when we slap multiplayer on top of it? Does it become more fun? Well, yes, of course it does. Just imagine playing this against a friend versus playing this alone. If you really picture this in your mind, then without a doubt, you'll agree with me. The multiplayer version is significantly more fun. Does that mean that you should only make multiplayer games? No. Firstly, for local multiplayer games, there's very low demand. Not a lot of people are looking for local multiplayer games on PC, at the very least. And secondly, online multiplayer games are very hard to produce. It's very hard to get them running properly. If you manage to set it all up and get it running, then multiplayer is usually more fun. The situation where I think this is probably the most dangerous is when you have multiple prototypes and you have to decide which one you want to keep working on. Your single-player prototype might have a way better game system behind it, but the multiplayer component of the other game will trick you into thinking that it is a lot more fun than it actually is. So you might make the wrong call. Every game is initially more fun as a multiplayer game. However, you cannot fix a bad game just by adding multiplayer. Eventually, all of that hollowness and lack of proper game design will come through, and multiplayer won't save you. I think my clicker game prototype demonstrates that quite well. The multiplayer component makes it a lot more fun initially, but with such a boring game system behind it, it will still get old very soon. If you do have a proper game system to back it up, if you do have a couple of very good game mechanics behind it, then I'm absolutely convinced multiplayer can be one of the most fun-inducing things ever. The second fun hack that pretty much makes every game significantly more satisfying to play is satisfying feedback. ## Level Design Does NOT Start With Any Level!
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9oAUX8Xp2Kw

Good level design starts before you design a single level. Unfortunately, I had to learn that the hard way with my game Spoontastic Baby. I made a big level design mistake, the game failed, and in this video I want to share with you what I think went wrong so you don't need to make the same mistake. The goal of the game is to feed the baby. Unfortunately, it doesn't want to be fed. It spits, it shoots fire, it has laser eyes, it's basically the devil that even eats your spoon every now and then. So it's basically a little baby boss fight game. We wanted players to keep playing the game so there is an infinite amount of levels and every level is slightly harder than the level before. One thing I realized even back then when I made the game was that levels need to be very different and unique, otherwise it would get pretty boring pretty soon. And the way I went about solving that issue was to randomize the baby's stats in every single level. The stats that probably made the most impact were the frequencies of the different attacks. So in some levels the player is only attacked by lasers, in other levels the player is only attacked by fire, and then once again in different levels the baby might use a variety of different attacks. We have 7 attack patterns so in theory this should result in a ton of possible combinations, right? Wrong, wrong, wrong, wrong, wrong. The thing I missed in my thought process was that those attack patterns are not really combined. They're still happening one after another. Doesn't matter how we rearrange them, it's the 7 exact same building blocks every single time. The result was that the levels were pretty boring and the game failed. So the first takeaway from this project is that level design is really your best friend if you want to create a lot of content and that's simply due to the fact that rearranging and recombining existing mechanics is a lot more efficient than creating entirely new ones. Secondly, make sure it is possible to recombine your mechanics in meaningful ways. In my game Overcharge I have blue turrets, green turrets, but I can also combine them and have both at the same time. Depending on how I rearrange these turrets as a level designer it will result in a completely different experience and challenge for the player. You know in which game that is absolutely not the case? Yeah. Also recombineability is not a binary thing. It's not like you have it or you don't. There are a lot of steps in between. Some mechanics might have some interesting interactions with each other and others might not. Your goal is obviously to get this net as dense as possible because that makes it easier to create interesting and varied levels. One way I tried to make the interaction between green and blue turrets more interesting in Overcharge for example was by giving green turrets the ability to slow down enemies. This way blue turrets have more time to shoot them as well. So synergies like that are what you're looking for. Third thing I've learned from Spoontastic is that you've got to leverage context. Once again if you look at Overcharge we can see that this turret has an entirely different context than this turret or than this turret. So depending on their surroundings and depending on their context they feel different to use for the player. You know in which game that is absolutely not the case? Yeah. The easiest way to create context in my opinion is the terrain. But only if your game objects have interesting interactions with the terrain. These presents for example use the terrain to move so yes they have interactions with the terrain, not super interesting ones but they do. These fireworks on the other hand don't interact with the terrain at all. That reduces the reusability of that mechanic quite a lot because we can't give it a different context or at the very least not a vastly different one. Of course there are other ways to give something context as well. For example the rounding objects. If you want to have any chance at creating quality levels you've got to make sure you have a good toolbox and a good set of building blocks that can actually be used and recombined in interesting ways. I'd love to keep exploring this topic in future videos and obviously I'll link them here once there's something out. Sorry that this video was a little short, I'll try to get healthy soon. Hope this helps you to avoid some of the mistakes I've made in the past. Let's discuss it in the comments and see you in the next one.

## How to make your game 2X as fun! - (In No Time.)
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=plj09H-aLOk

You can easily double the fun factor of your game with almost zero effort. There are a couple of tricks in game development that give you an insane amount of bang for your buck, both for your gameplay as well as for your visuals. I used to make games at this quality level all the time when I was younger, and I remember being pretty much stuck there. Back then, I wish I would have known what I'm about to tell you right now. Let's start simple. Let's start by analyzing the most frequent decisions the player has to take in your game. In this case, the most frequent decisions are where do you go and do you use your primary or your secondary fire? Your job as a game developer is to make these micro decisions as interesting as possible. At the moment, let's face it, both of them are pretty boring. It doesn't really matter where you go, and it doesn't really matter which fire mode you use. You can either run in circles or camp in the same corner for the entire match. It makes almost no difference in terms of outcome. Whenever you see a group of enemies, you use your bombs. When you see single enemies, you use your laser. So that's not really an interesting decision either. A micro decision needs two things in order to be interesting in my opinion. First of all, there needs to be a best solution, a best option to take, because if everything works equally well, the decision really doesn't matter. That's currently the issue with the movement. Doesn't matter where you go because everything works just fine. Secondly, it should be challenging to figure out what the best solution is. At the moment, it's pretty obvious which fire mode is better in each given situation. That turns the decision into something the player just does without even thinking about it. That's pretty boring. Here's what you can do about it. Add trade-offs and make options more unique. The trade-off I decided to use here is you are 50% slower whenever you use your laser and you can't move at all while firing your bombs. That makes the fire modes more different from one another, more unique, which makes the decision more interesting. But what's even better, it adds a third option and that is not firing at all. If you want to move at your maximum speed, you need to stop shooting. That also goes very well together with the next mechanic I decided to add. There are now these goal objects scattered on the map that you need to collect in order to score points. There are always two of them so you can decide where you want to go to. Bam! Your movement matters now and your fire mode matters even more. Using the bomb fire mode means you're not getting any closer to the goal objects and sometimes you even have to stop shooting altogether because you need the extra speed. You have to decide do you go straight to the next goal or do you clean house first? Which ring do you want to collect first and what's the best path to get there? I think you can tell that this already made the game so much better and I think you can also tell that this is absolutely possible for your own video game. Just identify the core decisions the player has to take in your game and find ways to make those decisions more interesting without adding an insane amount of complexity to your game. Remember there needs to be a quote-unquote best solution but it shouldn't be obvious what the best solution is. That's how you make these micro decisions more interesting and that's how you bring your gameplay to the next level. Next thing that gives you an insane amount of bang for your buck is just picking decent colors. It's usually not a lot of work. You don't need to change anything about your sprites. You just need to change their colors. Coming up with a good color scheme yourself is quite challenging so I recommend you just use one from the internet. Also look I'm not claiming this color scheme is already perfect by any stretch of the imagination. All I'm saying is this can give you a massive visual improvement in a very short amount of time. However my games always used to look like this and I see a lot of game jam games from you that look like this as well. There's no need for that. Just invest like 30 minutes into the colors and you can have something that looks a lot more like a finished game and a lot less like a prototype. Next thing you should absolutely do to increase the fun factor of your game is experimenting with the speed of your game. I often feel like games by unexperienced developers including myself when I was younger by the way are often way too slow. Pacing is obviously super important for games so just run a couple of experiments make your game 10% faster 20% faster 40% faster and see if any of those still works. In this case I got away with making the game 50% faster that's what you see right here. Faster is not necessarily always better but in most cases it means less downtime and more action. Next thing that can up your game with a minimal amount of effort is directional effects. Yes I also changed the color of the effects which makes them look a lot juicier but what I'm really trying to show you here is that the effects are now rotated they have a specific direction they are no longer just circles like before but they react to the direction the enemy was last shot at from. You don't need a combat based game to do something like this. Whenever you have visual effects or particles like this in your game make them react more to the player's actions and to the environment. They are a lot more interesting to look at if they are not exactly the same every single time. So more dynamic and reactive effects can juice up your gameplay a lot and in most cases they are not that hard to implement. At this point I realized that I wasn't quite satisfied with the colors. The color of these goal objects right here didn't quite fit in in my opinion. In case you ever have doubts like that as well it's probably just a good idea to reduce the amount of colors even further or at the very least that's the fastest way to fix issues with your color scheme. Next trick that gives you a massive amount of bang for your buck is camera movement. Here I just added a tiny amount of camera movement and some screen shape of course and it already makes the game feel a lot more dynamic and alive. After getting used to the new faster game speed you sometimes realize that the game is still pretty slow and could be even faster. In that case just speed it up again. Don't show all buttons right from the beginning. Unlock them one after another so the UI doesn't look cluttered and confusing when you get started.
And then later on when you're further into the game, it's way easier to handle that additional complexity.
If you want your players to feel smart, unlock one feature at a time. Don't show everything at once.
Now we're getting to the really interesting stuff. Make an easy game that feels hard.
Let's face it, games that feel hard feel rewarding and games that are hard are frustrating.
To get the best from both, you need to make a game that feels hard while actually being relatively easy.
In other words, you should try to fool players into thinking your game is a lot harder than it actually is.
Because if they manage to beat it, they'll feel a lot more accomplished and smarter this way.
Games that feel hard but also are hard in reality kind of have both. The frustrating part as well as the reward factor.
This is a valid approach as well. Dark Souls is a good example for that.
The worst case scenario is a game that looks easy while actually being quite hard.
Those are the games that drive me crazy the most and I feel like I'm not the only one.
Let's take the game Snake Path as an example. It looks super friendly and easy, there are no enemies nearby and the music is happy as ever.
But climbing this rock here was actually extremely hard for me. I had to try so many times and it made me feel really stupid.
Because it didn't even look like it was supposed to be a challenge. The game communicated to me, it's relatively easy to get up here and most players should be able to do this without any problems.
My experience however didn't quite match that message which made me feel quite stupid.
And yes, that's probably because I actually didn't do so well, I kind of was too stupid to get up there. But if possible you should still avoid making your players feel that way. Even when it's their fault, right?
So what could have fixed this part of Snake Path for me? I think if the game designers realized during playtesting that a couple of players got stuck at this point for a little too long, they should have simply put a couple of danger signs around the rock.
There should have been something that communicates it's actually a little tricky to get up here.
That's a win-win because if I manage to do it the first attempt, I feel smart and accomplished. And if I keep falling again and again, I don't feel that stupid because I can see this part is supposed to be a little tricky.
Best case scenario for most use cases in my opinion, make things look harder than they actually are.
Prevent people from getting stuck. Nobody likes getting stuck. You know why? Correctly, it makes you feel incompetent and stupid.
Very linear games suffer from this the most because you literally can't experience the rest of the game if you can't get past a certain section.
So firstly you should provide your players with some mental support so they keep trying. Show them that it's normal to get stuck every now and then. Maybe even do something smart like giving them an achievement for getting stuck.
And secondly help players to get unstuck. For example you could have a gameplay structure that allows players to progress in different routes or with different levels.
In an adventure game the main character could start dropping hints if you don't manage to make any progress for a while. Just something like maybe I should check out the graveyard again?
Just prevent players from getting stuck. You want players to feel competent not incompetent.
Then another thing you can do to make your players feel smarter is to help them through potentially frustrating parts of your game.
Sometimes having slightly frustrating parts in your game is just unavoidable. There are some acceptable things you can patch over these frustrating parts though to make them more enjoyable.
Firstly make it look harder than it is. But we already covered that. Secondly tease the player and tell her that there's something interesting and rewarding when she manages to make it through this part of the game.
Thirdly show the player that it's okay and normal to fail. For example you could trigger a funny new voice line every time you fall down a cliff.
And this just shows the player the developers already knew this was going to happen because the same thing probably happened to other players here

## Flow in Video Games
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bFoKKuMrHrQ

If you're into game development, you have definitely heard about the word flow. But what is flow? Why does it matter and how do you create flow? I want to share with you my favorite takeaways from this book as well as some of my own thoughts. Why does flow matter? The reason is experiencing flow is super duper fun. Understanding what flow is and how it works will firstly help you to make better games and secondly will also help you to make your own life more enjoyable. Now, what is flow? Flow is the state of optimal experience. You experience it when you're completely in the moment, focused on one task, you forget everything, you even forget yourself, you become one with the activity, you forget about time, everything disappears but just doing. And the moment appears that is actually super duper fun. You just do something and then suddenly three hours later you're like, what? Three hours already? That felt like 10 minutes. Then the next question is when does flow occur? What are the conditions for flow? And the first thing you usually see when we talk about that is this graph right here. If you want to get into flow, that means your skill has to match the challenge. If you are really skilled at something, then you also need a really high challenge. If you're very bad at something, then you obviously need a pretty small challenge. If your skill is way higher than the challenge, then you're in the boredom sector, then you're way too good for what you're supposed to do and you're just bored. When the challenge is way higher than your skill, then you're in the stress sector where you get anxious and you can't deal with the challenge anymore. Both boredom and stress is not fun. What's fun is exactly this flow funnel in the center right here. By the way, the further you climb that ladder, the more enjoyable it gets. Skill needs to match challenge, the first condition for flow. Then another condition is that you need to be completely focused on that activity. Your complete attention needs to be on that one thing. You cannot get into flow when you're distracted. If you think about something else and there's something else going on in your head, then there's no way you can get into flow. And then the last really important condition for flow is you need to know how well you're doing. That means you need to get feedback in some shape or form for how well you're performing. And usually what's super helpful for this is having a goal. Because if you have a goal, you can judge, did I get closer to that goal? Did I get further away from that goal? And that provides you with a constant stream of feedback. Pretty immediate feedback is the best. If you do something and then two hours later somebody tells you that was good or that was bad, it doesn't really give you as good of an experience as doing something and instantly getting feedback in the very same second if you performed well or poorly. And the cool thing about this is that our brain can do this by itself to some degree. For example, if I do some creative work and I paint something, my brain can give me feedback on how well I'm doing. Because I know what I want to create and I have a certain opinion of what looks good and then my brain can tell me, oh, that looks good or that doesn't look good. And basically you can provide that feedback to yourself. So let's repeat three conditions for flow to occur. The challenge needs to match your skill. Secondly, the challenge requires your full attention and you give that challenge your full attention and you need to know how well you're doing at the moment. Now let's get to the interesting question. How do we actually apply this to games? How do we create flow in games? First point, the challenge you present the player with needs to match the skill of the player. That means you need to get the difficulty curve completely right. Start your game out easy and then get progressively harder and harder and you need to do it exactly in the same speed that the player learns. The problem with that obviously is that this is extremely hard to predict and everybody is a little different. So that's one of the reasons why there are difficulty settings in a lot of games. That's why there are often additional challenges you can take. So if the level is too easy, you can try to get some additional pickups that are really hard to get or you can try to find some secrets. And then some games also have adaptive difficulties. They see how well you're performing. If you're performing poorly, they make the game easier. When you're performing pretty well, they make the game harder. Avoiding downtimes because downtimes basically mean the challenge doesn't match the skill of the player. The same goes for the opposite. Avoid high difficulty peaks. Make sure a player is ready before you present them with a challenge. Some people do this by putting a really hard enemy at the entrance of a dungeon so the players cannot enter the dungeon if they don't have the skill to beat that first enemy. Because if they went in there and they aren't skilled enough yet, they wouldn't enjoy that dungeon. So that's just a way to protect them from themselves. And then another point is don't make the player play boring parts of your game over and over again. That's one of the reasons why I think selling checkpoints is really important. Because yeah, that bit of the level might be challenging the first time you go through it. But if you go through that for the 10th time or for the 20th time, then it becomes really easy and boring. Then the next point, make sure the player can focus on the challenge. Unfortunately, that's not something that's completely in your control. It also depends a lot on the situation of the player. Some people just get distracted easily and they have a harder time to get into flow. What you can do is provide them with clear visuals, clear graphics, a non-distracting soundtrack. And that's pretty much all you can give them a motivation to focus. Online games do a really good job at that because there's a lot of peer pressure. You don't want to let your teammates down. You want to perform really well though. There's some sort of motivation to focus. So that helps. But honestly, there's not all that much you can do about that. Just hope that your players will focus. Then the last and really important thing you need to do is provide the player with clear feedback. You need to tell them how well he's doing. Is he performing well or poorly? Have clear goals and tell the player at every moment, yeah, you're doing a great job or that wasn't so nice. And also abuse the fact that the player can do that him or herself. And you need to do it in a way that allows the player to focus on the action, on the task. So the feedback shouldn't be distracting. It should be built into the experience in a way. Imagine an action game and whenever you hit an enemy, there's a text pop up that says, hey, cool, you hit the enemy and that's 70 damage. That's so awesome. Great job. And then you need to click on OK and then the game keeps going. Make sure the feedback is integrated in your game in a smart way. Then another really interesting question that the book talks about a lot is how do you use flow to make your own life more enjoyable? Being able to create a flow experience depends on two things. Firstly, on the activities or the game you're playing or whatever you're doing. And then the second thing is yourself. And we have talked about the first one. You know, the activity needs to provide you clear feedback. You need to know how well you're doing and your skill needs to match the challenge. But what do you need to do to get into flow? Firstly, you need to see everything as a challenge. Let's say you have to clean your room. And some people, they don't see any challenge in cleaning their room. And so they don't like it. They think it's boring. While on the other hand, somebody who sees it as a challenge and thinks, wow, how can I improve the order in my room? How can I make this a better place? Then it actually suddenly becomes a pretty hard challenge and one that is way more likely to actually match your skill. That way you can enjoy it a lot more. So whatever activity you're presented with, if it's washing dishes, if it's work in the garden, whatever it is, if you can find a challenge in that activity, you're way more likely to enjoy that activity. Then the second thing is you need to be able to control your attention. This is a pretty hard one. People nowadays have really short attention spans, myself included. So let's use the same example, cleaning your room. It's really hard to stay focused for 20 minutes on that and only that and not get distracted or sidetracked by anything. ## 7 Game Development Facts - Let's Face It!

Seven facts every game developer has to face. When I started making games I had a really romantic view about how all of this works, but let me tell you things are not that simple. Number one, your first game will not succeed. That depends on how you define success, but it will not be the next Minecraft or anything like that. Don't have any expectations, the odds are just packed against you. I've made a ton of games in my life and I still think that the game I'm currently working on will probably not succeed. Number two, making a game requires a lot of real hard work, it's not all fun and dandy. In the beginning you make a lot of quick progress and it goes really fast, but in the end it really slows down and drags on. There are so many little things you need to do to really finish your game, to make it a complete experience, all the menu and UI stuff takes so much time. So yeah, making games is really work. Number three is nobody cares about your game. If you want people to be excited about your game, you need to make them excited about your game. They won't just magically start caring about your game. In general they just don't care. The fourth thing you realize after making a couple of games is that you have almost infinite competition. There are so many games out there, digital distribution has made it so easy to make and publish games. They are literally billions. That means you need to make something really special and you need to be really smart about your distribution. Otherwise you don't really stand a chance. Number five is nobody will find your game. I always had this romantic view that oh if I make something really cool and really good people will find it automatically. That's not the case. They won't find it. They are not searching for your game. They don't know your game exists. They are not going to find it just by pure magic. That's just not how it works.
